rows.text: Monetary Policy Direction for 2017
(This English version was prepared by the Bank of Korea staff)
The 'Monetary Policy Direction for 2017' is published in accordance with the provisions of Article 6 of the Bank of Korea Act, and upon resolution by the Monetary Policy Board.

<The Bank of Korea Act> Article 6 (Setting of the Operational Direction for Monetary and Credit (1) The Bank of Korea shall set a price stability target in consultation with (2) The Bank of Korea shall set and publish the operational direction for monetary and credit policies every year.
(3) The Bank of Korea shall do its best to achieve the price stability target as provided for in Paragraph (1).
Ⅰ. Monetary Policy Environment in 2017
Ⅱ. Monetary Policy Direction for 2017
I. Monetary Policy Environment in 2017
While it is forecast that the domestic economy will maintain a modest trend of growth, the high uncertainties continue.
The pace of recovery in the global economy is forecast to pick up somewhat.
It is expected that the US economy will continue its expansion, Chinese economic growth will remain at the 6% level, and the sluggishness in natural resource-exporting countries will ease.
The domestic economy is expected to maintain its growth rate in the 2% range.

Although the sluggishness of exports is likely to ease along with the modest recovery of the global economy, and facilities investment to shift to an increase, the paces of growth in private consumption and construction investment will slow.
With the GDP growth trend falling below its potential level, the GDP gap is forecast to remain negative.
Meanwhile, the high uncertainties surrounding domestic and external conditions continue.
On the external side, economic stimulus policies in major countries will likely serve as positive factors.

There are substantial downside risks as well, however − for example of continued monetary policy normalization by the US Federal Reserve, of spreading protectionism, and of a possible slowdown in Chinese economic growth.
On the domestic side, there is a possibility of the contraction in economic confidence stemming from the political uncertainties working as a downside risk to growth.
Inflation is expected to gradually rise toward its target level.
Consumer price inflation will gradually rise toward the target,* in line with the increase in international oil prices and the weakening of concerns about global deflation.

However, with the demand-side inflationary pressures not large, as the GDP gap remains negative, it is forecast that the underlying trend of inflation including core inflation will be a little below 2%.
The movements of international oil prices and exchange rates will work as factors causing uncertainties to the future price path.
* The inflation target for 2016-2018 is 2.0% in terms of CPI (year-on-year).
3. Financial and Foreign Exchange Markets
In the financial and foreign exchange markets, the volatilities of foreign investment flows and price variables may increase.
The volatilities of capital flows and price variables may increase, affected by uncertainties related to the incoming US government
administration's policy directions, to the pace of the US Fed's increase of its policy rate, and to the Brexit.
Especially, if the financial and foreign exchange market unrest in EME countries deepens, there is a possibility of substantial negative effects spreading to the domestic markets.

However, the possibility of Korea experiencing any abrupt surge in outflows of foreign securities investment is not expected to be large, given Korea's favorable external soundness thanks to its ample foreign reserves and current account surplus.
The resilience of financial institutions is favorable overall, but the rapid increase in household debt remains a major financial sector vulnerability.
The household debt issue remains a major vulnerability in the financial sector, as the supply of credit to the household sector continues to increase.

Although the pace of sharply increasing bank lending to households is expected to slow, a trend of substantial growth at a level exceeding that of recent years is still forecast, owing for example to extensions of group loans for purchases of apartments under construction.
There are concerns that, if interest rates rise or household incomes worsen, then the debt repayment difficulties of low-credit, low-income and multiple debt holding borrowers may increase.
It is forecast that the upward trend in housing sales prices will slow, due to an expansion in the number of available apartments and to the government's measures to stabilize the housing market.
There are however both upside and downside risks to this forecast.
Factors giving rise to uncertainties about management conditions at financial institutions remain.
Among them are the buildup of household debt, increases in corporate credit risk, and changes in the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy.
However, financial institutions' resilience is expected to maintain favorable levels overall, as for example their capital adequacy ratios are far exceeding the regulatory requirements.
In conducting monetary policy, the Bank will maintain its accommodative policy stance while also paying attention to financial stability.

The Bank will work to strengthen its monetary policy communication, by for example publishing the General Principles of Monetary Policy Operation, and will increase effectiveness in the management of its lending facilities.

The Bank will strengthen its monitoring of developments in the financial and foreign exchange markets and its analysis of systemic risks in the financial sector, and respond proactively if any concerns about instability arise.
The Bank will operate the Base Rate so as to ensure that the recovery of economic growth continues and consumer price inflation approaches the inflation target over a medium-term horizon.
economic growth is forecast to be modest, and inflationary pressures on the demand side to therefore not be high, the Bank will maintain its accommodative monetary policy stance.

While keeping in mind the sharp increases in uncertainties surrounding internal and external conditions, the Bank will closely monitor the developments of risk factors and consequent changes in financial and economic conditions.

The Bank will in addition assess the underlying movements of inflation based on a wide range of indicators, including consumer prices as well as core inflation, various auxiliary price indices,* inflation expectations, the GDP gap, and indicators of slack in employment and manufacturing capacities.

The Bank will operate its monetary policy while paying attention to the risks to financial stability, for example from increased market volatility following the US Federal Reserve's increase in its policy rate, and from the accumulation of household debt.

The Bank will strengthen its monitoring of the trends of capital flows, the movements of price variables in the financial and foreign exchange markets, and developments related to household debt and corporate credit.

The Bank will publish the General Principles of Monetary Policy Operation, in order to help maintain consistency in its monetary policy communication and enhance the general public's understanding of the Bank's policy implementation.

The General Principles set forth the main purposes of monetary policy as defined in the Bank of Korea Act, the relationships between those purposes and the various factors to be considered in policy operation, and the basic policies employed to meet the purpose.

These General Principles will be included in the Monetary Policy Report, and when establishing its annual monetary policy direction every year the Bank will consider whether to revise and supplement them.

The Bank of Korea Act stipulates the goal of monetary policy as follows: "The Bank shall contribute to the sound development of the national economy through ensuring price stability, while giving due consideration to financial stability in carrying out its monetary policy."
In order to enhance transparency, predictability and effectiveness of monetary policy, the Bank will carry out its task by setting specific targets and objectives in accordance with this goal.
The Bank of Korea maintains a flexible inflation targeting system to effectively achieve price stability, which is the primary objective of monetary policy.
The inflation target is currently set at 2.0% in terms of consumer price inflation (year-on-year).
The inflation target is meant to be achieved over a medium-term horizon, since consumer price inflation is affected not only by monetary policy but also by
various other factors at home and abroad, which entail transitory and irregular impacts and the lag in monetary policy
The Bank conducts its monetary policy in a forward-looking manner, while considering symmetrically the risks of inflation remaining persistently above or below the target.
The path of convergence of inflation toward the target is assessed on overall inflation and growth outlooks as well as their uncertainties and risks, and on financial stability conditions.
The Bank conducts its monetary policy to support real economic growth to the extent that this does not hinder attaining the inflation target over the medium-term.
In ensuring price stability over the medium-term, the Bank pays careful attention to the impact of monetary policy on financial stability.

As persistent financial imbalance could undermine macroeconomic stability, paying due attention to financial stability in conducting monetary policy is consistent with the rationale behind flexible inflation
The Bank examines, assesses and announces financial stability conditions on a regular basis, to prevent excessive buildup of financial imbalances that may be brought about by monetary policy

Since there are limits to maintaining financial stability solely by monetary policy that indiscretely affects the whole economy, monetary policy needs to be complemented by macroprudential policies to prevent accumulation of financial imbalance.

The Bank will improve the content and method of presentation of its monetary policy statements to as to strengthen the explanation of the backgrounds behind its policy decisions and the signals of its future policy
While maintaining consistency with the announced general principles, the statements will also be written in a way that enhances their connections with the economic outlooks.
The scope of disclosure of materials from the MPB meetings for determining the policy directions will be expanded, through the Monetary Policy Report and press releases.

The Bank will step up its efforts to carry out research and study on the effects of the evolving financial and economic conditions and on effective countermeasures in response, and publish more related reports and materials.

Topics will include the effects of economic structural changes such as population aging on financial, economic and monetary policies, desirable policy responses to changes in the global environment, and the operation of monetary policy in consideration of the risks to financial

If consumer price inflation deviates from the target by more than ±0.5%p for six consecutive months,* the Bank will maintain its accountability for explaining this through for example press conferences held by the governor.
Explaining of the reasons for such deviation, the future inflation
outlook and the monetary policy operational directions for achieving the target will help in the anchoring of general inflation expectations.
If inflation continues to deviate from the target by more than ±0.5%p after that, then the Bank is required to provide further explanations of this every three months.

The Bank, in overall consideration of economic and financial conditions at home and abroad as well as SME funding conditions, will work to support the recovery of growth and an expansion of the growth potential through use of the Bank Intermediated Lending Support Facility.
The Bank will strengthen its funding support for SMEs suffering difficulties due to increased uncertainties at home and abroad, for SMEs having positive effects on employment, etc.

Especially, it will expand its liquidity support for regional SMEs experiencing temporary funding bottlenecks during the course of corporate restructuring, and ease the requirements for eligibility for support under the Support Program for High-tech and Other Start-up SMEs to support employment and growth.
The Bank will also provide support for sectors that can contribute to an expansion of the growth potential.
The Bank will review the overhaul of its lending programs from a medium- to long-term perspective, in reflection of developments in economic and financial conditions.

Along with overhauling the Bank Intermediated Lending Support Facility, the Bank will work to improve the guideline ratios for bank lending to SMEs in a way that enhances financial institutions' autonomy in their fund operations.
The Bank will prepare thoroughly for any possibilities of heightened financial and foreign exchange market volatilities caused by occurrences of shocks at home and abroad.
When financial market unrest surges, the Bank will respond decisively in order to stabilize the markets.
The Bank will closely watch developments related to risk factors, and more closely monitor capital flows, financial market price variables, and the behaviors of market participants.
The Bank will remain perpetually vigilant, while working actively to reflect any new changes in conditions in its contingency plans for preparing against financial and foreign exchange

The Bank will ensure that price variables such as interest rates and foreign exchange rates are fundamentally determined by market supply and demand, but will also take appropriate measures to stabilize the financial markets in cases of excessive herd behavior in the markets.
In any case of temporary financial market disruption due to an unexpected shock, the Bank will seek ways of mitigating it.

The Bank will strive to induce the revitalization of overnight RP transactions, and work with the government to modify the system for short-
term financial market regulation.
The Bank will communicate closely with the markets, to prevent any spreading of excessive anxieties in the financial and foreign exchange

While working to swiftly and accurately identify risk factors at home and abroad based on diverse information collected through market intelligence activities, and to firmly analyze their impacts, the Bank will communicate actively to the public its perceptions of financial and economic conditions.

When factors causing financial market instability arise the Bank will promptly convene ｢Financial and Economic Conditions Review Meetings｣ and ｢Monetary and Financial Task Force Meetings｣ for example, and swiftly explain to the public its perceptions of current conditions and its plans for response, through for example press releases or media interviews.
The Bank will work to enhance its capacities for responding to external shocks, by means such as strengthening the regional and global financial

The Bank will strengthen its financial cooperation by participating actively in the ASEAN+3's discussions related to enhancement of the CMIM functions and the G20's discussions on improving the IMF lending facilities, as well as by renewing its bilateral currency swap arrangements with other major country central banks.
In order to cope with the heightened uncertainties at home and abroad, the Bank will strengthen its examination of financial system stability.

The Bank will examine financial stability conditions more closely, by strengthening the Monetary Policy Board's regular ｢Macro-financial Stability Conditions Review Meetings｣, and enhance its function of early warning provision through the ｢Financial Stability Report｣.

While keeping a constant watch on household debt conditions by operation of its ｢Household Debt Task Force｣, the Bank will analyze from various perspectives the possibilities of household debt-related risks materializing, and devise plans in response.

In its joint banking examinations the Bank will focus on identifying and analyzing systemic risk factors, such as lending to vulnerable households and marginal firms and herd behavior in lending to specific sectors.
It will at the same time continue its efforts to alleviate the examination burdens of financial institutions.

The Bank will maintain its system for close cooperation with the government, the supervisory authorities, and international organizations such as the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI).

To cope with digital innovation and other factors, the Bank will work to facilitate the development of payment and settlement services and to constantly expand and improve the payment and settlement infrastructure.
The Bank will carry out a pilot program on introducing a 'coinless society' to enhance the convenience of the public and reduce social costs.
The Bank will establish foundations for the use of FinTech and distributed
ledger technology, and draw up measures to secure the safety and transparency of digital payment instruments.
It will meanwhile also carry out research in preparation for the possibility of digital currency issuance by the central bank.
The Bank will support the smooth launch and firm settlement into place of Internet-only banks, and devote efforts to minimizing any resulting occurrence of risks such as delays in payment and

To ease payment and settlement risk, the Bank will seek to ensure that more large-value funds transfers made via networks for small-value settlements are shifted to BOK-Wire+, and to reduce the net settlement amounts of financial institutions.
In an effort to enhance the settlement convenience of financial institutions and to reduce settlement risk, the Bank will extend the operating hours of BOK-Wire+.
It will also build an advanced payment and settlement risk management system, by for example preparing guidance on payment and settlement oversight.

In order to ease financial institutions' increased burdens of posting collateral for net settlement due to the strengthening of payment and settlement risk management, the Bank will consider expanding the range of securities accepted as collateral.
